headline: Town officials began planning for a potential FY28 operating override, raised transfer station fees, and approved major site variances for Costco.
synopsis: In July 2026, Southborough officials turned their attention to long-range financial planning, opening discussions on a potential five-year Proposition 2 1/2 operating override of up to $10 million to address a projected FY28 deficit. The Select Board approved higher transfer station fees for FY27, setting standard resident permits at $320 to cover increased hauling and operational costs. For public schools, architects presented a baseline conditions assessment for Neary Elementary School highlighting extensive infrastructure, ventilation, and accessibility needs. On the development front, the Zoning Board of Appeals granted setback and lighting variances for the proposed Costco on Coslin Drive and advanced a zoning amendment to update two-family housing rules. Meanwhile, the Board of Health approved updated well and septic regulations, and the Wastewater Study Committee decided to consult state regulators before bringing sewer proposals to Town Meeting.

top_items.title: Planning for potential multi-year FY28 operating override
top_items.why: Southborough faces a projected $2 million deficit in fiscal year 2028 that would exhaust remaining tax levy capacity. Town officials began discussions on proposing a five-year Proposition 2 1/2 operational override of up to $10 million.
top_items.body: The Select Board and Advisory Committee began reviewing long-range budget forecasts showing that Southborough will exhaust its remaining tax levy capacity in fiscal year 2028, with a projected $2 million gap. Officials discussed pursuing a five-year operational override rather than asking voters for annual overrides. The Advisory Committee debated whether override funding should be tied to municipal efficiency plans or directed toward long-term liabilities such as pensions and retiree healthcare. A joint meeting between the Select Board and Advisory Committee was set for August 11 to establish budget guidelines.

top_items.title: Transfer station sticker fees increased for FY27
top_items.why: The Select Board voted 5-0 to approve higher transfer station permit fees to cover operational and hauling expenses. The standard non-senior permit was set at $320, and senior permits were set at $75.
top_items.body: The Select Board adopted Option 2 for fiscal year 2027 transfer station permit fees following a presentation by the Department of Public Works. The approved rates set the first non-senior permit at $320, senior permits at $75, and second vehicle permits at $25, with hardship waivers remaining at $0. The increases are intended to offset operating costs, including $62,000 in contracted outside hauling while town staff obtain commercial driver's licenses. Proposed operational regulations restricting swap shop drop-offs and disposal of bulky items were postponed to August 11 for further review.

top_items.title: Neary School assessment outlines major facility deficiencies
top_items.why: Tappe Architects presented an existing conditions review showing that Neary Elementary School requires comprehensive system replacements, insulation, accessibility upgrades, and fire sprinklers. Designers are refining long-term options targeting Annual Town Meeting in 2027.
top_items.body: Tappe Architects delivered an initial existing conditions assessment of Margaret A. Neary Elementary School to the Elementary School Building Committee. The assessment concluded that while the core structure is sound and well maintained, the building needs significant capital investments, including modern triple-glazed windows, exterior wall insulation, full accessibility compliance, an automatic fire sprinkler system, and replacement of noisy unit ventilators with modern HVAC systems. The committee discussed educational space requirements, the condition of modular classrooms, and the possibility of moving school district administrative offices out of Neary.

top_items.title: Board of Health adopts new well and septic rules
top_items.why: The Board of Health voted unanimously to approve updated local rules for private wells and subsurface sewage disposal. The amendments require well water testing before real estate transfers and set a 25-foot well setback from swimming pools.
top_items.body: Following a public hearing, the Board of Health unanimously adopted revised regulations governing private drinking wells and subsurface sewage disposal systems. The new rules establish mandatory private well water testing prior to real estate transfers, require a 25-foot separation setback between wells and swimming pools, guarantee town access for septic repairs, and separate the professional roles of septic system design and system installation.

top_items.title: Zoning board approves retaining wall and lighting variances for Costco
top_items.why: The Zoning Board of Appeals voted 4-0 to approve variance relief for Costco Wholesale at 21 Coslin Drive. The decision permits retaining walls up to 31 feet high and parking lot light poles up to 36.5 feet.
top_items.body: Costco Wholesale Corporation received unanimous variance approval from the Zoning Board of Appeals to construct retaining walls up to 31 feet high within setback areas and install parking lot light poles reaching 36 feet 6 inches, exceeding the local 20-foot limit. Costco representatives explained that substantial retaining walls are necessary to navigate a 40-foot grade change across the former Dell campus to create a level parking lot. The taller light poles allow Costco to reduce the total number of light fixtures on site from 113 to 49 while keeping lighting dark-sky compliant with zero property-line spillover.

top_items.title: Rising project costs prompt increased CPA funding requests
top_items.why: Town committees presented revised Community Preservation Act applications for the Peninsula Trail footbridge, golf course irrigation, and Fay Memorial Park after cost estimates exceeded previous budgets. The applications were continued for updated filings.
top_items.body: The Community Preservation Committee reviewed revised funding applications for multiple capital projects facing increased costs. The Trails Committee requested an additional $178,496 in CPA funds for a pedestrian footbridge over the reservoir channel after adjusting project plans and dropping a boardwalk component, bringing the total bridge budget to $434,328. The Golf Course Committee presented an updated irrigation system estimate of $976,470, which includes a required booster pump station, proposing $100,000 from its revolving fund with the rest from CPA funds. The Recreation Commission also presented a $1.5 million plan for Fay Memorial Park that includes $240,000 in reconfigured parking. The committee continued the applications pending revised paperwork and warrant wording.

top_items.title: Zoning board advances two-family dwelling bylaw amendment
top_items.why: The Zoning Board of Appeals approved a draft zoning amendment clarifying regulations for two-family homes and eliminating a two-year conversion waiting period. The proposal was forwarded to the Select Board for referral to Town Meeting.
top_items.body: The Zoning Board of Appeals voted 4-0 to advance a draft zoning bylaw amendment governing two-family dwellings ahead of the October Special Town Meeting. The amendment creates a formal definition for two-family dwellings, distinguishes them from single-family houses with accessory dwelling units, updates minimum lot sizes across zoning districts, and removes an obsolete rule requiring owners to wait two years before converting single-family houses into two-family homes. The board referred the draft to the Select Board and Planning Board and scheduled a public informational session for August 12.

top_items.title: Wastewater committee pauses Town Meeting requests to consult MassDEP
top_items.why: The Wastewater Study Committee decided not to bring any funding articles or financing plans to the fall Special Town Meeting. The committee will first meet with state regulators to evaluate watershed discharge rules.
top_items.body: The Wastewater Study Committee agreed to hold an informational meeting with the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection to evaluate state watershed discharge restrictions under drinking water supply protection rules around the Sudbury Reservoir. The committee determined that establishing state regulatory limits for Zone C watershed discharge is required before conducting expensive field testing. Members also confirmed that Southborough will not submit a District Improvement Financing plan or any funding requests to the fall 2026 Special Town Meeting while it compiles financial feasibility models.
